lessons.body:
NIGERIAN STATE CAPITALS — FOUR ITEMS REQUIRED BY THE WEEK 1 ASSESSMENT

SUPPLEMENT STATUS
This is a small, original assessment-support supplement. It is deliberately labelled OUTSIDE SCHEME ROW 1 because the First Term Week 1 scheme row lists meaning, nature, scope and value of Geography, but does not include Nigerian state capitals. The source nevertheless asks for the capital of Lagos State in the General Evaluation and the capitals of Ebonyi, Plateau and Ogun States in the Theory question. This supplement teaches only those four capitals; it does not expand the scheme to all 36 states.

THE FOUR STATE–CAPITAL PAIRS

1. Lagos State — Ikeja.
2. Ebonyi State — Abakaliki.
3. Plateau State — Jos.
4. Ogun State — Abeokuta.

HOW TO STUDY THEM
Read each state name and say its capital aloud. Then cover the right-hand side and try to recall the capital. Remember that Lagos is a state and Ikeja is its capital; Abuja is the Federal Capital Territory, not the capital of Lagos State.

PRACTICE AND ANSWERS

Question 1 (4 marks): Write the capital of each state:
(a) Lagos
(b) Ebonyi
(c) Plateau
(d) Ogun

Answer:
(a) Ikeja
(b) Abakaliki
(c) Jos
(d) Abeokuta

Marking guide (4 marks total):
- Ikeja for Lagos — 1 mark.
- Abakaliki for Ebonyi — 1 mark.
- Jos for Plateau — 1 mark.
- Abeokuta for Ogun — 1 mark.

Question 2 (4 marks): Match each state to its capital:
Lagos; Ebonyi; Plateau; Ogun.
Options: Abeokuta; Ikeja; Jos; Abakaliki.

Answer: Lagos–Ikeja; Ebonyi–Abakaliki; Plateau–Jos; Ogun–Abeokuta.

Marking guide (4 marks total): award 1 mark for each correct state–capital pair. No half marks are needed.

SOURCE NOTE
The four capital pairs are checked against the National Bureau of Statistics' Nigeria map/table (Lagos–Ikeja, Ebonyi–Abakaliki, Ogun–Abeokuta) and the Independent National Electoral Commission's State Offices directory (Ebonyi–Abakaliki, Plateau–Jos, Ogun–Abeokuta). The original school-source questions are not changed. This supplement is new teaching content, not a claim that state capitals were in the Week 1 scheme.

lessons.title: The Solar System and the Universe
objectives: Define the solar system, universe, galaxy, satellite and orbit.
Name the eight planets in order from the Sun and distinguish rotation from revolution.
Describe important characteristics of the eight planets and explain Pluto's dwarf-planet classification.
Answer the Week Two source evaluation and theory questions using current, accurate astronomy.
lessons.body:
THE SOLAR SYSTEM AND THE UNIVERSE

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define the solar system, universe, galaxy, satellite and orbit; name the eight planets in order from the Sun; distinguish rotation from revolution; describe important features of each planet; and explain why Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet.

1. The solar system
The solar system is the Sun and all the objects held by its gravity that travel around it. These include eight planets, their natural satellites (moons), dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and smaller bodies. The Sun is a star. It supplies most of the light and heat used by the planets. The planets do not produce their own visible light like the Sun; they reflect sunlight.

A planet follows a path called an orbit around the Sun. Planetary orbits are elliptical, which means they are slightly oval rather than perfect circles. Revolution is the movement of a planet around the Sun. Rotation is the spinning of a body on its axis. Earth takes about 365¼ days to complete one revolution and about 24 hours to complete one rotation.

2. The eight planets in order
Starting nearest to the Sun, the eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. A memory aid is: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles.

Mercury is the smallest planet and the nearest to the Sun. It has no moon. Its surface becomes very hot in daylight and extremely cold at night because it has almost no atmosphere to retain heat. It is not the hottest planet.

Venus is the second planet from the Sun. It is similar to Earth in size and is sometimes called Earth's twin, but its surface conditions are very different. Its thick atmosphere traps heat, making Venus the hottest planet. Venus has no moon and rotates in the opposite direction to most planets.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun. It has one natural satellite, the Moon. Earth is the only world on which life is known to exist. Liquid water and a life-supporting atmosphere are among the conditions that make life possible. Earth has gravity, but gravity is not unique to Earth; all objects with mass exert gravity.

Mars is the fourth planet. It is often called the Red Planet because iron-rich dust gives much of its surface a reddish appearance. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

Jupiter is the fifth planet and the largest planet in the solar system. It is a gas giant with bands of clouds and a very large storm known as the Great Red Spot. It has many moons.

Saturn is the sixth planet. It is a gas giant best known for its broad and bright ring system. The rings are made mainly of pieces of ice and rocky material; they are not simply three solid rings. Saturn also has many moons.

Uranus is the seventh planet. It is an ice giant with a blue-green appearance. Its axis is tilted so far that it appears to rotate on its side. Its rotation is retrograde, meaning opposite to the direction used by most planets.

Neptune is the eighth and most distant of the eight planets from the Sun. It is an ice giant with a very cold atmosphere and extremely fast winds.

3. Pluto and the dwarf planets
The original school note calls Pluto the ninth planet and includes it in a table of nine planets. This is an outdated classification. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as an object that orbits the Sun, is nearly round because of its own gravity, and has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. Pluto meets the first two conditions but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood. It is therefore classified as a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets. Pluto remains an important member of the solar system.

4. The universe, galaxies and satellites
The universe includes all space, time, matter and energy. It contains an enormous number of galaxies. A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity. Our solar system is in the Milky Way galaxy. The Milky Way contains far more than a few dozen stars; it contains hundreds of billions of stars.

A satellite is an object that moves around a larger body. A natural satellite is not made by people. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. Artificial satellites are built by people and placed in orbit for purposes such as communication, weather observation and navigation.

5. Important corrections to the older source table and descriptions
Use the eight-planet classification, not a list of nine planets. Pluto is a dwarf planet. Mercury is nearest to the Sun but Venus is the hottest planet. Earth is the only planet currently known to support life, but oxygen and gravity are not exclusive to Earth. Saturn has a complex ring system, not only three rings. Uranus is not accurately described as the only planet rotating clockwise; its axis is extremely tilted and its rotation is retrograde. Counts of moons change as new moons are confirmed, so learn the stable facts above rather than memorising the old source table's satellite counts. Distances and orbital periods in the source table are approximate and should not be treated as precise current measurements.

6. Answers to the source evaluation and theory questions
A solar system is a star and the objects that orbit it under gravity. Our solar system includes the Sun, eight planets, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.
A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity. A satellite moves around a planet or another larger body. An orbit is the path followed by an object as it moves around another body.
The universe is the totality of space, time, matter and energy; it contains galaxies, stars, planets and many other objects.
One characteristic of each planet: Mercury is the smallest and nearest to the Sun; Venus is the hottest; Earth has liquid water and is the only known world with life; Mars is reddish and has two moons; Jupiter is the largest; Saturn has prominent rings; Uranus rotates on a strongly tilted axis; Neptune is the most distant of the eight planets.
The first four planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Mercury is small and nearest the Sun; Venus is second and hottest; Earth is the third planet and has one Moon; Mars is the fourth and appears red.
The last of the eight planets is Neptune. It is farthest from the Sun among the eight planets and has a cold atmosphere with very fast winds.
Earth's natural satellite is the Moon.

7. Source question review
The source asks which statement is not true: that all planets 'rotate around' the Sun or that they 'revolve around' the Sun. The wording is ambiguous because 'rotate around' is sometimes used informally to mean orbit, while rotation properly means spinning on an axis. Do not score this item until it is rewritten as: 'Which statement correctly describes a planet's revolution? Answer: It moves around the Sun along an orbit.'
The source asks which two planets lie between the Sun and Earth. The answer is Mercury and Venus.
The source asks which planet has the largest orbit and offers Pluto. Under the current classification, Pluto is a dwarf planet; among the eight planets, Neptune is farthest from the Sun. Rewrite the item to ask 'Which of the eight planets is farthest from the Sun?' Answer: Neptune.
The source asks which planet has no satellite and gives Venus, Uranus and Neptune as options. Venus is the correct option among those choices; Mercury also has no moon.
The source calls Venus Earth's twin because of similarities in size, mass and density. Venus is similar in size to Earth, but its environment is extremely different.

PRACTICE
1. Define solar system, galaxy, satellite and orbit.
2. List the eight planets in order from the Sun.
3. Explain the difference between rotation and revolution.
4. State one important characteristic of each of the eight planets.
5. Explain why Pluto is a dwarf planet rather than one of the eight planets.
6. Why is Venus hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is nearer to the Sun?
7. Name Earth's natural satellite and state two uses of artificial satellites.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Solar system: the Sun and objects that orbit it under gravity. Galaxy: a huge system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held by gravity. Satellite: an object that moves around a larger body. Orbit: the path followed by an orbiting object. Award 1 mark for each correct definition (4 marks).
2. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (4 marks; 0.5 mark each in order).
3. Rotation is spinning on an axis; revolution is movement around another body, in this lesson a planet moving around the Sun. Award 2 marks for each clear definition (4 marks).
4. Award 1 mark for one accurate characteristic for each named planet, up to 8 marks. Accept the characteristics in section 2.
5. Pluto orbits the Sun and is nearly round, but it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood; the IAU therefore classifies it as a dwarf planet (3 marks).
6. Venus has a dense atmosphere that traps heat through a strong greenhouse effect; Mercury has almost no atmosphere to retain heat (3 marks).
7. The Moon (1 mark). Artificial satellites are used for communication, weather monitoring, navigation, Earth observation or scientific research; award 1 mark for each of any two (3 marks).

Total: 29 marks. Teachers may adapt the total while preserving the stated item-level marking.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement based on the school's First Term Geography Week Two topic and assessment prompts. It preserves the source's topic sequence but corrects outdated or inaccurate astronomy claims rather than reproducing them as current facts. The original source document remains unchanged.
The International Astronomical Union's 2006 Resolution 5A and Resolution 6A classify the eight planets and Pluto as a dwarf planet: https://www.iau.org/IAU/Iau/News/PR2006/iau-2006-general-assembly-resolution-votes.aspx
NASA Solar System Facts confirms the solar system has eight planets and describes the Milky Way: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/solar-system-facts/
NASA Mercury Facts confirms Mercury is nearest to the Sun and not the hottest planet: https://science.nasa.gov/mercury/facts/
NASA Venus Facts identifies Venus as the hottest planet: https://science.nasa.gov/venus/venus-facts/
The school's reading pointer 'Essential Geography, O.A. Iwena, pages 5-7' is recorded in the source, but that book was not supplied for inspection; the page range and its contents are not independently verified by this supplement.

lessons.title: Earth as a Planet: Shape, Size and Movements
objectives: Describe Earth's approximate shape and size using accurate measurements.
Explain evidence that Earth is approximately spherical.
Define rotation and revolution and describe their effects.
Explain how Earth's axial tilt and revolution produce seasons, changing daylight and eclipses.
lessons.body:
EARTH AS A PLANET: SHAPE, SIZE AND MOVEMENTS

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to describe Earth's shape and size; explain evidence that Earth is not flat; distinguish rotation from revolution; describe the effects of each movement; explain the role of axial tilt in seasons; and define dawn and twilight.

1. The shape of the Earth
Earth is approximately spherical, but it is not a perfect sphere. It is slightly flattened at the North and South Poles and bulges around the Equator. This approximate mathematical shape is called an oblate spheroid. The word geoid is also used in geography, but it has a more precise meaning: it describes an irregular surface related to Earth's gravity field that closely matches mean sea level extended beneath the continents. For simple classroom description, say that Earth is nearly spherical and slightly flattened at the poles; do not treat the geoid as a perfect ball.

2. The size of the Earth
Earth is the fifth-largest planet in the solar system. Its equatorial diameter is about 12,756 kilometres. Its polar diameter is about 12,714 kilometres. The equatorial circumference is about 40,075 kilometres. These values are approximate and may differ slightly between reference sources because of the way measurements are defined. The total surface area is about 510 million square kilometres. Earth is slightly wider across the Equator than from pole to pole because it rotates.

3. Evidence that the Earth is approximately spherical
(a) Photographs and measurements from space: satellites and spacecraft provide images and precise measurements of Earth's curved shape.
(b) Lunar eclipses: during a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and Moon and its shadow falls on the Moon. The curved edge of the shadow is evidence of Earth's round shape.
(c) Ships at the horizon: when a ship moves away, its hull disappears before its mast; when it approaches, the mast may become visible before the lower part of the ship. This is consistent with a curved surface, although visibility, waves and atmospheric conditions also affect what an observer sees.
(d) Circumnavigation: people and ships can travel around the world and return to their starting region without meeting an edge. The expedition led by Ferdinand Magellan began the first circumnavigation in 1519. Magellan died before it was completed; Juan Sebastián Elcano led the surviving expedition back to Spain in 1522. It is therefore inaccurate to say that Magellan personally completed the voyage.
(e) Different stars and horizons: observers at different latitudes see different parts of the sky and different apparent altitudes of stars. The horizon also changes with the observer's position and height.
(f) Geodetic surveys: measurements using satellites, GPS and surveying instruments establish Earth's curved, slightly flattened shape.

4. Rotation of the Earth
Rotation is the spinning of Earth on its imaginary axis, an imaginary line running through the North and South Poles. Earth rotates from west to east. One rotation takes approximately 24 hours when measured from one noon to the next; relative to distant stars it takes about 23 hours 56 minutes. For SS1 calculations, use 24 hours unless a question states otherwise.

Earth turns through 360 degrees in about 24 hours. Therefore:
- 360° ÷ 24 = 15° per hour.
- 15° ÷ 60 = 0.25° per minute.
- 1° corresponds to about 4 minutes of time.
Places east of another place generally experience local noon earlier because Earth rotates eastward; places to the west experience it later.

Main effects of rotation
1. Day and night: the half of Earth facing the Sun has daylight; the half turned away has night. Rotation carries places into and out of sunlight.
2. Apparent daily movement of the Sun and stars: the sky appears to move from east to west because Earth rotates from west to east.
3. Differences in local time: places at different longitudes face the Sun at different times. The approximate relationship is 15 degrees of longitude per hour, or 1 degree per four minutes.
4. Deflection of moving air and water: Earth's rotation contributes to the Coriolis effect. Moving air and water are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The effect influences large-scale winds and ocean currents; it does not mean every small moving object visibly curves.
5. The daily cycle of tides: the Moon's gravity, and to a lesser extent the Sun's gravity, produce tidal forces. Earth's rotation carries coastal locations through changing tidal conditions. Rotation alone does not create the tides.

5. Revolution of the Earth
Revolution is the movement of one body around another along an orbit. Earth revolves around the Sun and completes one orbit in about 365.2422 days, commonly written as approximately 365¼ days. The Moon revolves around Earth. Earth and the Moon travel together around the Sun.

A calendar year normally has 365 days. The extra fraction of a day is managed by leap years. In the Gregorian calendar, a year divisible by four is usually a leap year; a century year is not a leap year unless it is also divisible by 400. A leap year has 366 days.

Main effects of revolution together with Earth's axial tilt
1. A year: the time Earth takes to complete one orbit around the Sun defines the length of the year.
2. Seasons: Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit. As Earth revolves around the Sun, each hemisphere is tilted towards or away from the Sun at different times. This change in the angle and duration of sunlight produces the seasons. The Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons. Seasons are not caused by Earth simply being nearer to or farther from the Sun.
3. Changes in the Sun's midday height: the Sun appears higher or lower in the sky at midday at different times of the year because of Earth's axial tilt and orbital position.
4. Changes in day and night length: outside the Equator, the length of daylight changes through the year. The amount of change depends on latitude; near the poles, periods of continuous daylight or darkness can occur.
5. Seasonal temperature changes: the angle and duration of incoming sunlight affect heating. Local weather, clouds, oceans and land also influence temperature, so seasons are not identical everywhere.

6. Equinoxes, solstices, dawn and twilight
An equinox occurs when the Sun is positioned over the Equator and day and night are approximately equal in length across much of Earth. A solstice occurs when the Sun reaches its greatest apparent northward or southward position; these dates mark the longest and shortest daylight periods in each hemisphere.
Dawn is the period of increasing light before sunrise. Twilight is the period when sunlight still illuminates the sky after sunset or before sunrise, even though the Sun is below the horizon. Dawn and twilight are not the same as sunrise and sunset.

7. Eclipses
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and blocks all or part of the Sun from view for observers in the Moon's shadow. A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth is between the Sun and Moon and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. A solar eclipse occurs at new Moon and a lunar eclipse at full Moon, but they do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun.

8. Answers to the source evaluation and theory questions
Earth's shape: approximately spherical, more precisely an oblate spheroid; geoid is the gravity-related reference surface close to mean sea level.
Earth's size: equatorial diameter about 12,756 km; polar diameter about 12,714 km; equatorial circumference about 40,075 km; surface area about 510 million km². Earth is the fifth-largest planet.
Four proofs of Earth's sphericity: images and measurements from space; Earth's curved shadow during lunar eclipses; ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon; and circumnavigation. Other acceptable evidence includes geodetic surveys and changes in the visible sky with latitude.
The Magellan expedition began the first circumnavigation in 1519; Magellan died during the voyage. Elcano led the surviving expedition that returned to Spain in 1522.
Rotation means spinning on an axis. Its effects include day and night, apparent daily movement of celestial objects, local-time differences and the Coriolis effect. Tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun, while Earth's rotation helps create the daily pattern experienced at coasts.
Revolution means movement around another body. Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun. Together with axial tilt, revolution produces the yearly pattern of seasons and changes in day length and the Sun's midday height.
The Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. This is an apparent motion caused mainly by Earth's west-to-east rotation.

PRACTICE
1. Describe Earth's shape. Explain the difference between an oblate spheroid and the geoid.
2. State four measurements or facts that describe Earth's size.
3. Give five pieces of evidence that Earth is approximately spherical.
4. Define rotation and state four effects of Earth's rotation.
5. Define revolution and explain why Earth has seasons.
6. Distinguish an equinox from a solstice.
7. Explain the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse.
8. Correct this statement: 'Magellan was the first person to sail around the world and personally completed the journey.'
9. A place is 30° east of Greenwich. Using 15° per hour, calculate its approximate local-time difference from Greenwich.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Earth is nearly spherical and slightly flattened at the poles; an oblate spheroid is the smooth mathematical approximation, while the geoid is an irregular gravity-related surface close to mean sea level. Award 2 marks for shape and 2 for the distinction (4 marks).
2. Any four: equatorial diameter about 12,756 km; polar diameter about 12,714 km; equatorial circumference about 40,075 km; surface area about 510 million km²; fifth-largest planet. Award 1 mark each (4 marks).
3. Any five valid proofs from section 3, each briefly explained (5 marks).
4. Rotation is spinning on an axis (2 marks). Award 1 mark each for four valid effects (4 marks). Total 6 marks.

practice.q: Describe Earth's shape. Explain the difference between an oblate spheroid and the geoid.
practice.answer: Earth is nearly spherical and slightly flattened at the poles; an oblate spheroid is the smooth mathematical approximation, while the geoid is an irregular gravity-related surface close to mean sea level.

practice.q: State four measurements or facts that describe Earth's size.
practice.answer: Any four: equatorial diameter about 12,756 km; polar diameter about 12,714 km; equatorial circumference about 40,075 km; surface area about 510 million km²; fifth-largest planet.

marking.criterion: Four correct size facts or measurements

practice.q: Give five pieces of evidence that Earth is approximately spherical.
practice.answer: Any five: images and measurements from space; Earth's curved shadow during lunar eclipses; ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon; circumnavigation; geodetic surveys; changes in the visible sky with latitude.

marking.criterion: Five valid pieces of evidence, briefly explained

practice.q: Define rotation and state four effects of Earth's rotation.
practice.answer: Rotation is spinning on an axis. Effects include day and night, apparent daily movement of celestial objects, local-time differences and the Coriolis effect.

practice.q: Define revolution and explain why Earth has seasons.
practice.answer: Revolution is Earth's movement around the Sun along an orbit. Seasons occur because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4°; as Earth revolves, each hemisphere receives different angles and durations of sunlight.

practice.q: Distinguish an equinox from a solstice.
practice.answer: An equinox occurs when the Sun is over the Equator and day and night are approximately equal. A solstice occurs when the Sun reaches its greatest apparent northward or southward position, producing the longest or shortest daylight period.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse.
practice.answer: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun. A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth is between the Sun and Moon and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

practice.q: Correct this statement: Magellan was the first person to sail around the world and personally completed the journey.
practice.answer: Magellan led the expedition that began in 1519 but died before it finished; Juan Sebastián Elcano led the surviving crew back to Spain in 1522.

marking.criterion: States Magellan led the expedition but died before completion
Identifies Elcano as leader of the returning survivors

practice.q: A place is 30° east of Greenwich. Using 15° per hour, calculate its approximate local-time difference from Greenwich.
practice.answer: 30° ÷ 15° per hour = 2 hours. A place east is ahead, so the local time is approximately 2 hours ahead of Greenwich.
